questions.stem: What does X <=_p Y formally mean?
choices: There is a polynomial-time function f such that I in X iff f(I) in Y
X has fewer instances than Y
X and Y have the same algorithms
questions.explanation: Polynomial-time (Karp) reduction: f maps instances, and the answer is preserved in both directions.

questions.stem: Polynomial-time reductions are transitive: X <=_p Y and Y <=_p Z imply:
questions.explanation: Composing two polynomial-time reductions yields another polynomial-time reduction. Transitivity is central to chaining hardness.

questions.stem: If Y has a polynomial algorithm and X <=_p Y, what follows?
questions.explanation: Translate I to f(I) in polynomial time, run Y's algorithm. Gives X in P.

questions.stem: Independent Set <=_p Vertex Cover uses which mapping?
choices: (G, k) -> (G, n - k); S is IS iff V \ S is VC
questions.explanation: S is independent iff its complement V \ S is a vertex cover. Hence the IS/VC duality is a 'simple equivalence' reduction.

questions.stem: Independent Set <=_p Clique uses which mapping?
choices: (G, k) -> (G-bar, k) where G-bar is the complement graph
questions.explanation: S is IS in G iff S is a clique in the complement graph G-bar.

questions.stem: Which best describes the 3-SAT to IS gadget reduction?
choices: Triangle per clause + conflict edges between literal and its negation; k = number of clauses
questions.explanation: Each clause gets a triangle (one node per literal); conflict edges connect x and not-x across triangles. IS of size m exists iff phi is satisfiable.

questions.stem: Why is k = m (number of clauses) in the 3-SAT to IS reduction?
choices: An IS can take at most one node per triangle, so a satisfying assignment selects one literal per clause -> exactly m IS nodes
questions.explanation: Each triangle contributes at most one IS node; total of m. Setting all chosen literals to true satisfies the formula.

questions.stem: A 'reduction by special-to-general' shows hardness by:
choices: Embedding the known-hard problem as a special case of the target
questions.explanation: VC <=_p Set Cover by treating edges as universe and vertex incidence-sets as cover sets — VC is a special case.

questions.stem: Vertex Cover <=_p Set Cover maps:
choices: Edges as universe; each vertex induces a covering set of its incident edges
Vertices as universe and edges as covering sets
questions.explanation: Universe = E, sets = {S_v : v in V} where S_v contains the edges incident to v. k-vertex cover iff k-set cover.

questions.stem: What must be proved in both directions in a reduction?
choices: Forward (yes -> yes) and backward (yes -> yes), and polynomial-time construction
questions.explanation: Both directions of the iff plus polynomial construction time are required for a valid Karp reduction.

questions.stem: Which is NOT one of the three reduction strategies?
questions.explanation: Greedy refinement isn't a reduction strategy. Lecture 9 lists simple equivalence, special-to-general, and gadgets.

questions.stem: Why do we focus on decision problems for NP-hardness reductions?
choices: Decision, search, and optimisation are polynomial-time inter-reducible, so deciding suffices technically
questions.explanation: Decision <=_p Search <=_p Optimisation (and reverse with binary search). Decision is the canonical framing.

questions.stem: If 3-SAT <=_p X and X is in P, what follows?
choices: 3-SAT is in P (and consequently every problem in NP is in P -- contradicting common belief unless P = NP)
questions.explanation: 3-SAT is NP-complete; placing it in P collapses P = NP.

questions.stem: Conflict edges in the 3-SAT to IS gadget:
choices: Connect a literal node to a same-clause literal
Connect every literal x to every literal not-x across triangles
Connect every node to every other
questions.explanation: Conflict edges prevent picking inconsistent literal assignments across clauses. They are the second crucial part of the gadget.

questions.stem: What is true about a Karp reduction's runtime requirement?
choices: It must be polynomial in the size of the X-instance
questions.explanation: Polynomial-time = polynomial in the bit-length of the X-instance, by definition.

questions.stem: Which problem is NOT one of the standard NP-complete problems chained from 3-SAT in this unit?
questions.explanation: Bipartite Matching is in P (solvable by max-flow). The others are NP-complete.

questions.stem: In a 'gadget' reduction, what is a gadget?
choices: A small constructed structure encoding a single input element's constraints in the target problem
questions.explanation: Each variable, clause, or input element is realised as a small target-problem fragment whose local structure enforces the original semantics.

questions.stem: Why is the 3-SAT to IS reduction's gadget set k = m (not n)?
choices: k = m corresponds to 'one true literal per clause' = satisfying assignment
questions.explanation: Satisfying assignment picks at least one true literal per clause; picking exactly one per triangle gives an IS of size m.

questions.stem: Which combination of facts is needed to chain hardness from problem A to problem C via B?
choices: A <=_p B and B <=_p C, both polynomial reductions
A in P and B in NP
A in NP-hard and C in NP-hard
questions.explanation: Transitivity: A <=_p B <=_p C gives A <=_p C. If A is hard, C inherits hardness.

questions.stem: The independent-set form of the 3-SAT reduction outputs an IS of size m iff:
questions.explanation: By construction the IS of size m maps to a consistent literal choice (one per clause) that satisfies every clause.

questions.stem: Suppose you found a polynomial algorithm for IS. What would follow?
choices: Vertex Cover and 3-SAT would also be in P; eventually P = NP
questions.explanation: IS is NP-complete. A polynomial algorithm collapses the entire NP class into P.

questions.stem: In the reduction recipe, which step is OPTIONAL?
choices: Implement the target algorithm in code
questions.explanation: The reduction is a mathematical translation; coding the target algorithm is not part of the proof.

questions.stem: Karp reductions are also called:
questions.explanation: Karp reductions are many-one (mapping) polynomial-time reductions. Cook (Turing) reductions are more general (multiple oracle calls).

questions.stem: Why does proving X <=_p Y certify that Y is 'at least as hard as' X?
choices: Solving Y solves X with polynomial overhead — so if Y were easy, X would be too
questions.explanation: Reductions inherit polynomial-time solvability from target to source — equivalently, they propagate hardness from source to target.

questions.stem: Which of these is the BEST way to prove a new problem Y is NP-hard?
choices: Pick a known NP-hard X and construct a polynomial-time reduction X <=_p Y, proving both directions
Find an exponential algorithm for Y
questions.explanation: NP-hardness is established by reducing FROM a known NP-hard problem TO Y. Showing Y in NP is separate (used for NP-completeness).
